title: Wojtek — the bear the Polish army enlisted
sources: Wikipedia: Wojtek — Syrian brown bear (1942 – 2 December 1963); on 8 April 1942, on the journey from Pahlavi to Tehran, Polish soldiers of Anders' Army met a young Iranian boy who had found a bear cub whose mother had been shot by hunters; 18-year-old refugee Irena (Inka) Bokiewicz prompted Lieutenant Anatol Tarnowiecki to buy him; donated to the 2nd Transport Company (later 22nd Artillery Supply Company), named Wojtek by the soldiers; fed condensed milk from an old vodka bottle; often rewarded with beer, his favourite drink; wrestled with the soldiers, was taught to salute, slept with soldiers if they were cold at night; British transport ship regulations to Italy forbade mascots and pets, so he was officially drafted as a private of the 22nd Artillery Supply Company, with his own paybook, rank and serial number; during the Battle of Monte Cassino he carried 100-pound (45 kg) crates of artillery shells, never dropping any — the story's accuracy is debated, but at least one account exists of a British soldier recalling a bear carrying crates of ammunition; he copied the men lifting crates; promoted to corporal; the company adopted a bear carrying an artillery shell as its emblem; after the war went to Scotland with the company, then on 15 November 1947 to Edinburgh Zoo, visited by former Polish soldiers; he still responded to being spoken to in Polish
Wikipedia: Battle of Monte Cassino — final capture cost over 43,000 Allied casualties; the first flag raised over the ruins of the monastery, on 18 May 1944 at 10.20, was the Polish flag

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / Imperial War Museum / Polish National Digital Archive): Wojtek with a Polish soldier; Wojtek as a cub in Iran; Wojtek wrestling soldiers of the 22nd Company; Wojtek at Winfield, Berwickshire, after the war; the 22nd Company badge; Polish II Corps unloading artillery shells at Monte Cassino, May 1944; Polish and British flags over the monastery ruins; the ruined monastery, 19 May 1944
Archive film (public domain): 'The Battle of San Pietro' (US Army Pictorial Service, 1945) — Allied trucks, guns and shellfire in the Italian mountains, 1943 — illustrative only, not Wojtek's unit

post.facebook:
The Polish army gave him a paybook, a rank and a serial number. He was a bear.

In April 1942, Polish soldiers on the road to Tehran met a boy with a bear cub whose mother had been shot by hunters. An 18-year-old refugee, Irena Bokiewicz, talked an officer into buying him. The soldiers named him Wojtek. He drank condensed milk from an old vodka bottle — and, as he grew, beer became his favourite drink.

When the 2nd Polish Corps sailed for Italy, the British transport ship allowed no pets. So the Poles enlisted him: Private Wojtek, 22nd Artillery Supply Company.

At Monte Cassino in 1944 his company hauled shells to the guns — and Wojtek, copying the men, is said to have carried 45-kilo crates of artillery shells without dropping one. Historians still argue about it, but at least one British soldier remembered seeing a bear carry ammunition. He was promoted to corporal, and his company's badge became a bear carrying a shell.

After the war he lived out his life at Edinburgh Zoo. Old comrades came to visit and spoke to him in Polish — and he still answered.

Would you believe it? 🐻

The Polish army gave him a paybook, a rank and a serial number. He was a bear.

Wojtek was adopted as a cub in Iran in 1942. To get him onto a British ship to Italy — no pets allowed — the 2nd Polish Corps enlisted him as a private of the 22nd Artillery Supply Company. At Monte Cassino in 1944 he is said to have carried crates of artillery shells, copying the men around him. Promoted to corporal, he became his company's badge, and ended his days at Edinburgh Zoo, where old comrades still spoke to him in Polish.
